articles.title: Tiny critically endangered puddle frogs born at London Zoo
articles.summary: The Afia Birago’s puddle frogs are a recently identified species from a single Ghanaian forest.
articles.content:
Ben Tapley, curator of reptiles and amphibians at ZSL, which runs the central London zoo, said: "They may be tiny enough to sit on your fingertip, but their arrival represents a huge step forward for an amphibian facing an uncertain future."

ZSL said no other zoo or institution was known to keep the species.

It was only described by scientists in 2018. Fully grown, the frogs weigh less than 1.75g.

ZSL said almost nothing was known about them when they arrived, and keepers have since developed breeding techniques that are being shared with the CSIR-Forestry Research Institute of Ghana's breeding centre in Kumasi.

The aim is to build up a population in Ghana that could be released into the wild.

Ghanaian conservationist Caleb Ofori-Boateng, who helped identify the species, named it after his mother, Afia Birago.

"I named this frog after my mother so that her legacy would live on," he said.

"Thanks to this breeding programme, it will. Her name will be linked to a species we saved, not one we lost."

The births follow the zoo's success last November in breeding the Atewa slippery frog, another critically endangered species from the same forest, which had also never been bred in captivity before.

articles.title: Pampered city trees deal with stress better than their country cousins
articles.content:
The next time you pass an urban tree, stop to appreciate what it’s been through. As a youngster, it was especially vulnerable to pests and diseases, not to mention vandalism. Now grown up, it must contend with ever-rising temperatures due to the heat island effect — the built environment’s tendency to soak up solar energy and slowly release it at night.

You might assume, then, that city trees are by default worse off than their rural counterparts. But new research suggests that urban vegetation is more resilient than you might think. Using satellite data from 2001 to 2022, researchers found that in more than three-quarters of 751 cities worldwide, plant life better coped with climate stresses like extreme heat than greenery in the surrounding countryside. In one-third of those municipalities, trees showed a “dual advantage,” losing less greenness from pressures in the first place, but also recovering faster from them.

That’s allowing metropolitan vegetation to do what it does best: reduce temperatures by providing shade, boost biodiversity by creating habitats, and mitigate flooding by allowing rainwater to soak into soil instead of pooling on concrete. “Generally, the urban environment is harsher for vegetation — for example, the air temperature and also the air pollution,” said Zhengfei Guo, an ecologist at the University of Hong Kong and lead author of a new paper describing the research. “Therefore, our results that found urban vegetation is more resilient than rural vegetation is very surprising.”

So what’s going on here? The researchers reckon this increased resiliency comes down to something no tree can thrive without: water.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

If you’ve ever seen your local parks department or a nonprofit plant a tree on the street, you might have noticed them placing a plastic bladder around its trunk. This provides consistent water for the sapling to help it grow big and strong in its most vulnerable years. Elsewhere in the metropolis, crews make sure that green spaces are sufficiently hydrated. And in backyard gardens, residents use hoses or drip irrigation systems to keep their flora verdant.

The built environment itself is inadvertently helping here, too. The traditional way of designing a city called for funneling water into sewer systems as quickly as possible to prevent pooling and flooding. As rainwater cascades off buildings and sidewalks, it flows into patches of dirt with trees, where it can soak into the ground.

Which is all to say: Urban vegetation is often pampered compared to what’s growing wild in the countryside. This is an advantage in the long term, but doubly so during relentless droughts and increasingly miserable heat waves. While rural trees desiccate, their compatriots in cities are regularly attended to. “They’re showing this kind of great ability to be resilient, most likely from just intentional management from people, or just the way we’ve simply designed cities to move and work,” said Eric North, program manager for urban forestry at the Arbor Day Foundation, who wasn’t involved in the new research.

For many plants in the city, additional heat can actually help. The urban heat island effect raises temperatures perhaps 20 degrees Fahrenheit higher than in nearby rural areas, because all that concrete and brick holds onto the sun’s warmth. This is potentially deadly for people, on account of the mercury staying high through the wee hours and denying the body time to cool down and recuperate. (Indeed, nights overall are warming faster than days are.) But it can be advantageous for well-watered plants, because the phenomenon is also in effect outside of summer. This is extending growing seasons, providing some species with extra time to flourish.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Interestingly, while these researchers found that vegetation was overall more resilient in cities, it was more so in the urban core compared to the outer neighborhoods. One theory why is that the heart of a city tends to be more developed and parks more rigorously tended. “The urban edge is not as stable as the urban core,” Guo said.

However, just because all that greenery has been enjoying surprising resilience, that doesn’t mean it’s guaranteed to do so forever, as the impacts of climate change grow ever more dire. “Some new ways to think about how to better sustain the urban area will become more and more important,” said Jin Wu, an ecologist at the University of Hong Kong and coauthor of the new paper.

For one, cities are trying to prioritize planting native species, which may already be adapted to withstand drought. They’re also looking to hotter places, importing species that scientists already know work there — essentially getting ahead of the baking to come. Selecting trees that are both drought-tolerant and have large canopies brings a double benefit, as the additional shade protects the surrounding dirt. “I’m assuming that’s really what a driving factor here is,” North said. “That it’s keeping the moisture that’s in the ground locked in, instead of evaporating off the ground, and so it’s more available for plants to use.”

Cities are also getting smarter about water. Los Angeles, for instance, is building “sponge city” infrastructure, things like roadside green spaces that allow water to soak into the ground and collect in cisterns rather than flow into sewers. It’s also using spreading grounds — giant dirt bowls, basically, where rainwater is piped and allowed to percolate into the underlying aquifer, from which it can be pumped during the dry season.

With proper water management, cities can remain green in the challenging decades to come. They’re building out urban gardens, for example, which bring all the benefits of greenery in general and provide nutritious food for residents. Scientists are also growing crops on rooftops under the shade of solar panels, generating clean electricity and supersized vegetables.

In a weird way, then, cities are becoming more rural. Now we have evidence that with a little TLC, plants can ensure metropolises don’t just survive, but thrive.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on a significant scientific finding that urban trees are more resilient to climate stresses than rural trees, due to intentional human management and city design. This has broad positive implications for urban climate adaptation, biodiversity, and environmental sustainability, benefiting large populations worldwide. The article provides detailed context on the mechanisms behind this resilience and ongoing efforts to improve urban greenery, making it a substantive and inspiring environmental story.
articles.personality_title: City trees show surprising strength against heat and drought

**Impact** – This shows that trees in cities are not just surviving but thriving despite tough conditions. articles.title: Dog that hunts invasive 'sea vomit' honoured as animal of the year
articles.summary: Sgiath is thought to be the UK's first sea squirt-hunting dog and has been trained to sniff out the marine pest.
articles.content:
"When I first started this project, I genuinely didn't know whether it would work," said Sim.

"No one had really explored whether dogs could help tackle this problem in the marine environment. It began as a proof-of-concept project and has exceeded every expectation I had."

Dogs' scent detection skills are often used in conservation work on land, including tracking endangered species and helping investigate environmental crime. At low tide, Sgiath can, as Sim puts it "dive down under the seaweed".

"She just does a survey with her nose, essentially, she can pinpoint exactly where it is, so it's much easier," she said.

Marine experts believe that carpet sea squirt, formally named Didemnum vexillum, came from Japan. It arrived on the shores of the south of England and Wales in 2008.

It can appear in various shades - from orange to cream - and has now spread to several seaside locations across the UK.

It reproduces quickly during the warmer summer months and, with warming seas, there are fears it could spread further.

Dr Martyn Kurr, a marine biologist from Bangor University told BBC News that non-native or "biofouling" species, like the carpet sea squirt, can outcompete native wildlife for valuable nutrients.

"These species also clog up aquaculture pens, marine infrastructure, and machinery such as boat propellors," he explained.

Efforts to control and clean up these problematic marine invaders costs millions of pounds every year across Europe.
articles.reasoning: The article describes an innovative conservation effort using a specially trained dog to detect an invasive marine species, which has broad environmental significance by aiding in controlling a costly and ecologically harmful pest. This represents a meaningful, tangible environmental benefit with clear context and impact.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A specially trained dog is helping scientists tackle an invasive marine pest by using its nose to find and control the harmful sea squirts along UK shores.

articles.title: India and China aren't friends - but Nepal wants to unite them against climate threats
articles.summary: Can Nepal bring the two regional giants together to confront a shared climate threat in the Himalayas?
articles.content:
Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah used much of his speech at the recent UN General Assembly to warn of the growing threat of climate-related disasters in the Himalayas, recalling the devastating debris floods that struck his country in August.

But it was his ambitious proposal to bring together regional rivals India and China, alongside Nepal, to tackle these shared threats that drew particular attention.

Shah called for the creation of a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism to strengthen cross-border disaster response and the sharing of scientific data and expertise in one of the world's most environmentally fragile and geopolitically sensitive regions.

"Let the Himalayas become a laboratory of international co-operation rather than a frontier of fragmented information," he said.

A senior official at Nepal's foreign ministry, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the proposal was still at an early stage.

"The PM's proposal has given a political direction. Our ministry is working with other relevant agencies to put forward a preliminary framework which can be the basis for building common understanding," the official said.

Neither India nor China has formally responded to the proposal. The BBC has contacted their foreign ministries for comment.

But can Nepal really bring the two regional giants together to confront a shared climate threat in a region where they have long been locked in bitter territorial disputes?

India and China share a disputed frontier stretching roughly 3,500km (2,175 miles), much of it across the Himalayas. Their competing territorial claims have led to a war, deadly clashes and repeated military stand-offs along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the de facto boundary separating areas under their control.

But the mountains that have long been a source of friction between the two countries are also facing an urgent climate threat.

Temperatures in the Himalayan region are rising faster than the global average, accelerating glacier retreat and permafrost thaw and contributing to growing risks of landslides, rockfalls, avalanches and glacial lake outburst floods.

Such disasters can sweep across national boundaries, threatening lives, infrastructure and livelihoods far downstream - making co-operation between the countries sharing the Himalayas increasingly important.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on Nepal's proactive and ambitious proposal to unite India and China—two regional rivals—to collaboratively address urgent and shared climate threats in the Himalayas. This initiative, if successful, could lead to significant cross-border cooperation on disaster response and scientific data sharing in a geopolitically sensitive and environmentally fragile region, representing a meaningful and hopeful step for climate action with broad regional impact.
articles.personality_title: Nepal proposes joint action by India and China to protect the Himalayas from climate risks

**Impact** – This idea is important because the Himalayas are fragile and disasters there can affect many people across borders. **One-sentence takeaway** – Nepal is trying to bring India and China together to protect the Himalayas from climate dangers by sharing knowledge and responding to disasters as a team.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Lors de la récente Assemblée générale des Nations Unies, le Premier ministre népalais Balendra Shah a proposé que l'Inde, la Chine et le Népal travaillent ensemble pour faire face à ces menaces climatiques. L'Inde et la Chine n'ont pas encore répondu officiellement. Les prochaines étapes seront de voir si ces pays acceptent de commencer à travailler ensemble sur ce problème commun.

articles.personality_title_es: Nepal propone acción conjunta de India y China para proteger el Himalaya de riesgos climáticos
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El Himalaya, compartido por India, China y Nepal, enfrenta crecientes peligros climáticos como inundaciones y deslizamientos debido a que las temperaturas aumentan más rápido allí que en la mayoría de los lugares. India y China han tenido largos conflictos fronterizos en esta región.

**Qué pasó** – En la reciente Asamblea General de las Naciones Unidas, el primer ministro de Nepal, Balendra Shah, sugirió que India, China y Nepal trabajen juntos para enfrentar estas amenazas climáticas. Propuso crear un Mecanismo de Resiliencia Climática del Himalaya para mejorar el intercambio de información y la respuesta a desastres.

**Impacto** – Esta idea es importante porque el Himalaya es frágil y los desastres pueden afectar a muchas personas a través de las fronteras. Si los tres países cooperan, podrán prepararse mejor para inundaciones y avalanchas, protegiendo vidas y hogares. También ofrece una oportunidad para que India y China colaboren a pesar de sus desacuerdos políticos.

**Próximo paso** – El gobierno de Nepal está trabajando en un plan para explicar cómo funcionaría esta cooperación. India y China aún no han respondido oficialmente. El siguiente paso será ver si estos países aceptan comenzar a trabajar juntos en este problema común.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Nepal intenta unir a India y China para proteger el Himalaya de los peligros climáticos compartiendo conocimientos y respondiendo juntos a los desastres.
